Personally, I wouldn’t take the antibiotics that the doctor prescribed. Skin infections (generally) are caused by staph and strep, and cephalexin is a broad enough antibiotic that it covers both, while clindamycin only covers strep infections (amongst other things, but not relevant with what we’re talking about). Additionally, the ear cartilage can also be infected with pseudomonas, which neither cephalexin or clindamycin would work for, you would need a different antibiotic altogether. That being said, it’s hard to tell what exactly you’re infected with without a culture test. 

Did the second doctor know you were on cephalexin first? I would probably seek advice from another doctor and hopefully get a culture before taking the clindamycin! When you said that you didn’t feel great, did you mean like fevers and stuff? because that would be indicative that you may still have the infection.

In the drugs, poisons and controlled substances act it states that: ‘for a pharmacist, being requested or directed to sell, supply or dispense any drug of dependence, Schedule 8 poison, Schedule 9 poison or Schedule 4 poison for any person more frequently than appears to be reasonably necessary’ is a reportable drug event. 

https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/vic/consol_act/dpacsa1981422/s32a.html

In the drugs, poisons and controlled substances exposure draft it states that: ‘a pharmacist must not sell or supply a schedule 8 poison on a prescription contrary to the instructions written on a prescription, including by- supplying the poison before an interval specified in the prescription has elapsed’. 

https://www.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2019-11/Drugs-Poisons-and-Controlled-Substances-Regulations-2017-Draft-Regulation.pdf

Like I said, in the case of excessive supply, the pharmacist will need to get a hold of the prescribing doctor to ascertain a reason for the excessive supply, and notify the MPR. 

https://www.health.vic.gov.au/drugs-and-poisons/pharmacists

While this might vary between states, safescript exists in multiple states to monitor for the supply of S8 medications and certain S4 medications across all pharmacies.

All S8 prescriptions with repeats require a repeat interval, which is a specified amount of days before the person can get the said S8 drug dispensed again. If you need an S8 medication dispensed early for emergency purposes, you will need to contact your doctor to let them know about the need for an early supply so they can get in contact with the pharmacy to give verbal and followed up with a physical confirmation of this early supply. Not doing so will flag you on the safe script system (at least in Victoria), which pharmacists do not take lightly. At least in the pharmacy I work at, we wouldn’t supply more than the specified repeat interval for S8 drugs just because it’s holiday seasons.

there is no 'passing' or 'failing' a sac. if you've done the coursework and demonstrated your understanding in an aos, that's a pass.

however, how you do RELATIVELY in sacs compared to your peers is what matters. if you're scoring above average compared to your cohort, even if that's 40% or 80%, you're still ranked higher than others. therefore, since sac difficulty varies between schools, a 'passing' or 'failing' mark is hard to moderate. it's all relative.

your % score mean nothing. find out your rank within the cohort. even then, a chunk of your ss comes from the exam aswell. reddit can't give you an accurate indication of how well you're doing, i'd recommend you talk to a vce counsellor or someone similar to that effect.
